body.x: Most people on Shia matchmaking sites are exactly who they claim to be: sincere seekers, often searching with their families beside them. But a small minority of profiles are not looking for a spouse at all. They are looking for money, for identity documents, or for someone whose hope can be converted into payments. Matrimonial sites attract fraudsters for a simple reason — the people on them are trusting, family-minded and ready to commit, and hope can be hurried in ways ordinary caution would never allow. This guide names the patterns that target rishta seekers, shows the point at which each can still be stopped, and explains what to do if one has already gone too far.
The borrowed face: fake profiles with stolen photographs

The photographs look genuine because they are genuine — they simply belong to somebody else. Fraudsters lift pictures from public social media: a model, a doctor, a soldier, sometimes an ordinary person whose holiday photos were never locked down. Beneath the borrowed face sits a profile engineered to be difficult to refuse — strong practice, good education, an impressive job in another city or another country, and a family situation kept just vague enough to explain why nobody local can vouch for them.

The tell is the video call that never happens. The camera is broken, the posting is remote, the connection is poor, the work is offshore — the excuse rotates for weeks. A real seeker, however shy, can almost always manage one short live video call, ideally with family present. Run a reverse image search on the profile photographs too; stolen pictures usually appear elsewhere, under other names. A profile that cannot be seen live, and cannot be found anywhere else in life, should be treated as fiction until proven otherwise.
The romance that turns into an investment

This pattern opens like a sincere courtship: attentive messages, religious language used correctly, serious talk of family and a future. Then, once trust is built, the subject changes. There is a trading platform that has done remarkably well. A cousin in finance. Screenshots of profits. The first suggestion is gentle — a small amount, just to see — and early withdrawals may even work, because the trap is baited. The real request comes later, when the sum is life-changing. Understand what has happened by then: the rishta was never the product. Your savings were. No genuine seeker needs you to invest in anything, and the moment a courtship produces a money-making scheme, the courtship is over — whatever it felt like.
The visa story and the sudden emergency

Here the match talks convincingly, often from abroad, and a crisis arrives on schedule. A visa fee must be paid today. An agent is holding the file. There is a medical emergency, a customs charge on a parcel sent for you, a ticket that must be bought before the price rises. The first amount is small and painfully plausible; each payment then creates the next problem, and each problem costs a little more than the last. Notice the mechanics: money is requested by wire transfer, gift cards or payment to a third party — routes chosen because they cannot be reversed. Genuine families handle their own emergencies and would be mortified to bill a stranger they hope to marry into. A money request in a rishta conversation is not a test of generosity. It is the entire point of the conversation, and it should end it.
The rush to move off the platform

Within a day or two, the new contact wants to continue on a private WhatsApp number or a personal email address. There are innocent reasons to do this eventually — but a fraudster has a specific one. On the platform, the conversation leaves a record, reports carry consequences, and a removed profile warns other families. Off the platform there is nothing to report and nobody to warn. Stay where the record exists until identity has been verified, family is involved, and the person has passed ordinary checks. A sincere seeker can wait a few weeks. A script cannot.
Hygiene that stops most fraud before it starts
None of this asks you to suspect everyone. It asks for fixed habits, applied to everyone equally, so that nobody has to be judged on instinct alone:

Verify identity early with a live video call, family present where possible, before personal details are exchanged.
Reverse-search profile photographs; borrowed pictures usually appear under other names.
Keep the conversation on the platform until identity is confirmed — on Shia Rishta, messaging opens on mutual interest, which already filters out casual and mass contact.
Never send money, gift cards, bank details, passport scans or visa documents to someone you have not met in person, with family involved.
Bring your wali or family in early; fraud depends on privacy between two people, and it wilts under a second pair of eyes.
Report and block at the first money request, and tell the platform exactly what happened — your report protects the next family.
If money or documents have already been shared
It happens to intelligent, careful people, because these scripts are built by professionals and aimed at hope. Shame is the fraudster's protection, not yours. Act quickly:

Stop all further payments and contact your bank at once; fast action sometimes allows a transfer to be recalled.
If identity documents were sent, treat them as compromised: alert your bank, watch for accounts or credit opened in your name, and inform the police.
Save everything before blocking — screenshots, receipts, profile names, numbers — because evidence vanishes when a profile is deleted.
Report the profile on the platform and, where money was lost, to your national fraud-reporting service.
Tell your family and warn your community discreetly; the same operator often returns under a new name within weeks.

None of these habits closes the heart. They simply restore the order traditional rishta searching always had: identity established through community, family involved from early on, and money nowhere in the conversation until two households are joining openly. Fraud borrows the language of sincerity. Sequence is how you tell them apart.
